I can't stress enough that this is my opinion, and in this community you are going to run into a lot of differing thoughts. So take this with a grain of salt.

There is such a hard learning curve with linux, and the large number of different groups and variants of linux can only complicate things. Your going to have to pick a particular distribution to start with.

A lot of users are going to push ubuntu, but it is rather reliant on a graphical user interface. I would like to stress that linux's strength is not central to a GUI, of which there are many. If you want to be proficient with it you should think about not even installing one at all. ubuntu is a great distribution, don't get me wrong, but as far as an operating system for proficient learning, it may not be the best. I would recommend you to look into RHEL or a free variant (CentOS or Scientific Linux).

Every distribution usually has documentation, some better than others. I will try to sidestep any arguments here and only point you to some documentation: https://access.redhat.com/documentation/en-US/Red_Hat_Enterprise_Linux/ http://www.linuxhomenetworking.com/wiki/index.php/Main_Page

Don't ever be afraid to ask a question to the community, via IRC, forums, etc. But do your research first, Google is your friend here. There will also be extensive documentation via what we call man pages, but they will only help when you know the command or program you want help with. The community can be a little harsh to new users, and learning how to asking specific questions with all the proper information will be of HUGE importance.

I wish you the best of luck.

Like others have said, Linux Mint is a great start. Personally, however, I love the Arch based package distribution, Pacman, and would advise you to consider Manjaro as a starting point. The latest iteration leaves you with a pretty sleek basic install.

Gaming performance is going to be far more dependent on your desktop environment than your particular distro and therefore I'd go for an xfce4 environment. Unless Valve manage to pull off some optimization magic with SteamOS, you will get better gaming performance from steam on a distro running xfce than with SteamOS itself.

edit: Also, as I don't think anyone has mentioned yet, make sure you use at least 2 partitions for your install. You should have a smallish (say about 20gb) root install (mount point /) and then a much larger Home directory (mount point /home). That makes it much easier for you to just jump in and try out a distro, because if you change distro you could leave your /home partition intact and keep all of your settings.

I'd highly recommend that you double and triple check to make sure all of your hardware works without issues in Linux. Most incompatibilities border on the 1 in a million chance and if there is a problem then there is almost always a fix or alternate option to get around it but for peace of mind make sure your GPU, gamer keyboards, mice, sound, network cards etc have no glaringly obvious issues before installing your distro.
